title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI-generated deepfakes were used to create a fake news article impersonating ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock. The fabricated interview promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, as part of a broader scam that used AI to generate convincing false content across multiple channels including fake websites and advertisements. This failure occurred in the deployment phase, where generative AI tools capable of producing realistic text and images were applied without restriction to financial fraud.

The scam was not caught before it circulated because there was no verification layer between content generation and publication. No human review appears to have checked whether the article's claims were accurate or whether the platform being promoted was legitimate. An effective catch would have required either public figures or financial regulators to verify media coverage before it reached potential victims, or platforms hosting the content to check credentials against official registers.

It is not established whether the AI systems were intentionally built for fraud or were repurposed by scammers after deployment for legitimate purposes.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has emerged as part of a rising trend of AI-generated investment scams. The fabricated article described a heated interview where Bullock allegedly stormed out over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. This type of scam uses deepfake technology to create convincing but false content designed to promote illegitimate investment opportunities.

ASIC reports that these sophisticated schemes are becoming increasingly common and harder to detect. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Gina Rinehart, and Alan Kohler are among the most frequently impersonated public figures. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements to lure investors. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its public registers and never invest if a business cannot provide legitimate credentials.
